642310.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
642310.value: Economics is largely the study of resource allocation. This proposed research project attempts to solve a puzzle concerning the optimal allocation of scarce resources to produce valuable commodities. If society’s objective is to produce the maximum amount of a valuable commodity, how should resources be allocated to the producers? Suppose that there is a continuum of producers and a fixed amount of resources is available. If producers are heterogeneous only in productivity, should more productive individuals receive more resources? Basic economic theory suggests that the resources should be allocated such that the marginal product is equalized across the producers. If there exist two producers whose marginal products are unequal, then one can take some resources from the producer with a lower marginal product and give them to the producer with a higher marginal product. The increase in output from the latter will exceed the decrease in output from the former. The maximum amount of commodity will be produced only if the marginal products are equalized. There is one important aspect of this theory that has not yet been studied. If the least-productive individual in the continuum of producers is nonproductive (i.e., the marginal product is zero for any level of input), what will be the optimal allocation of resources? Clearly, the non-productive individual should not be allocated any resources. However, it can be shown that, under some general conditions, not only the non-productive individual but also some of the low-productivity individuals should not be allocated any resources. On the other hand, if the least-productive individual is a little productive, then every producer, no matter how low his productivity is, should be allocated some resources. In other words, a low-productivity producer, who is not allocated any resources because the least-productive individual is non-productive, will be allocated some resources if the least-productive individual turns infinitesimally productive. This is a puzzling result. The productivity of the least-productive individual can alter the optimal allocation of resources in a remarkable way. The marginal product is not equalized across all individuals. The objectives of this project are to establish and solve the puzzle, examine whether and how the results can be applied to explain observed economic and social behaviors and to explore the policy implications. In addition, the research will investigate whether a similar puzzle appears in a popular production model with input prices. 作最優資源分配的理論分析，研究在連續生產者下，有或沒有生產力者存在的影響和分別。研究同樣的結果能否出現在一個更一般的結構。建立有明確解式的分析例子，去了解最優資源分配模型的特性。檢查可否或如何把最優資源分配模型應用於可見的經濟和社會行為，及其政策含意。加入原料價格於最優資源分配模型，與沒有原料價格的結果作比較。

642410.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
642410.value: This proposed project will be a key step towards developing a comprehensive understanding of the role of (siege) wars in late imperial China. It aims to reconstruct the size and costs of the Song-Mongol wars in thirteenth-century Sichuan and demonstrate an important impact of military mobilization upon the state’s financial structure. Furthermore, this empirical research will provide first-hand information for comparing China’s siege wars with their counterparts in early modern Europe regarding to the formation of state power. The role of warfare in the Chinese civilization has been ignored for a long time. In contrast, the rise of the west, scholars have argued, was closely associated with the emergence of European states that often resorted to violent means to strengthen their power. The aggressive monarchs in early modern Europe thus became friendly and even enthusiastic about economic development because the government could secure a large amount of tax revenues from the market to wage wars. This stereotype is in direct contrast to what really happened to Song China (960-1279), which was not only the richest country in the world but also fought the largest number of wars in imperial China. Meanwhile, Song China witnessed significant financial innovations, many of which should be attributed to the connection between commercialized warfare and the monetarized economy. The twelfth century was the most violent period in Chinese history, in which the Song dynasty enjoyed only 18 years of peace. Threatened by the nomadic invasions, the Song administration turned to siege wars: fortifications, engines, and projectile technologies. This extremely capital-intensive warfare forced the government, who was already hard-pressed by budget deficits, to appeal to the financial market for help. In the last three decades before the Mongols conquered China in 1279, the resistant wars in Sichuan provide an excellent example of how war makes states and vice versa. In Sichuan, more than half of the military expenditures were met by the issuance of Jiaozi and Chuanyin, the certificates of public debts that were backed up by official profits from a wine monopoly and by state reserves of precious metals. By 1256, the size of the public debt increased to 28 million strings, far exceeding what the Sichuan administration collected from taxing the local economy. This higher-level military-fiscal mechanism gave enormous strength to the Sichuan society in defense against invasions; Sichuan's government and troops did not surrender until the Mongols occupied all other parts of China. 本項目旨在重建13世紀四川面對蒙古入侵的抵禦規模和費用，以及由此所引起的重要財政變化。這對於深入理解戰爭、特別是城防戰，在中國歷史上的重大作用是至關重要的一步，也為比較中西歷史上城防戰的意義及其發展提供了第一手的數據資料。 戰爭在中國文明史上重要作用是一個極其重要卻常被忽視的問題。相比之下，學術界經常將西方的崛起與一個能夠訴諸暴力手段來獲取權力的近代國家之路聯係起來。因爲需要大量的稅收來維持戰爭費用，一個軍事上富於進攻性的歐洲君主也就親近市場，甚至鼓勵經濟發展。歐洲近代戰爭-財政國家之路和宋代中國的歷史有驚人的相似，後者不僅是當時世界上最富裕的國家，也經歷過中國歷史上數目最多的戰爭。 宋朝的許多金融創新起因于市場化的軍事動員模式和貨幣化的經濟生活。南宋時期（1127-1279）是中國歷史上戰爭最頻繁的時期，其中和平年份僅僅18年。面對遊牧民族的入侵，宋朝發展出城防戰的軍事抵禦體系，使用要塞建設、投射式武器製造等資本密集型抵禦手段。這種抵禦方式又給宋朝政府已經頗感壓力的財政提出更高的要求，而惟有發行公共債務纔是救急之道。在與蒙古人對抗的三十多年裏，四川一半以上的軍事費用是通過交子和川引的發行而提供的。它們其實就是一種由政府信用擔保的有價證券，而政府則以榷賣收入及貴金屬等為抵押。到1256年，此种公債的規模已經達到2千8百萬貫，遠遠超過四川地方經濟所貢獻的稅收。這種發達的財政-軍事體系為四川抵禦外侵提供了充足的資源，保證了諸多軍事上的勝利，而四川也是南宋境内堅持抵抗時間最長的地區之一。

642410.label: Realisation of objectives
642410.value: In my research I demonstrate a radical shift from an indirect-tax-based regime to a demonetized regime during the Song-Yuan_Ming transition and attribute it (such as changes in the sources and structures of public finance) largely to changes in the mode of military mobilization. This project, a tentative yet systematic investigation of Chinese financial history in the five centuries from 1000 to 1500, sheds lights on the political economy study of pre-industrial China. On this regard, the result achieved in this project exceeds what was originally planned, a case study of less-than-two-century-long siege warfare in Sichuan. The original project, a historical narrative of the siege wars in Sichuan in the Southern Song period, is to be fully accomplished in the next year (the final outcome will be a monographic study). The reason that I first concentrate on the macro-perspective research on pre-industrial China's state finance and military modes (rather than on a narrative on the local case in Sichuan) is the audience (mostly social scientists and European historians) are much more interested in what happened to China's financial systems as a whole, say, the difference between and after the Mongol conquest. In my original research plan, this is an important question but not addressed systematically. As I gave reports at the international conferences and workshops, this issue turned out fundamental to the entire research field. I thus shift focus from writing the story about the military defense in Sichuan to the comparison on the state finance between Southern Song and early Ming eras. I expect the Sichuan case study, when finished in the coming year (2015), will become persuasive as it is connected to the macro image. The major research outcome out of this project is an already finished book manuscript, namely, Wrestling for Power, the changing relationship between the market and the state in China, 1000-1500. In addition, I have published three research papers: one English paper at Economic History Review, a top journal in the field of economic history, and two Chinese papers.

642410.label: Major findings and research outcome
642410.value: The five centuries from roughly 1000 onward saw two distinct public financial systems taking shape in China during the reigns of the Song (960-1279) dynasty and the early Ming era (1368-1450), respectively. The shift from the former to the latter was not a smooth transition: the Mongol conquest of China and the subsequent period of its rule marked a sharp break in the development of the public financial system, which can be said to follow a Schumpeterian trajectory. In the context of the Song dynasty, this means that the state gained enormous fiscal strength by efficiently taxing the economy through indirect taxation and exploiting instruments of credits. This system came to an abrupt end in the late 13th century and was replaced by a command economy at the beginning of the Ming dynasty. Chinese economy was highly demonetized as the result of the early Ming rulers’ anti-market policies, and the structure of public finance retreated to a payment-in-kind system that largely relied on direct control of population and land. In each case, the making of the public financial system was closely intertwined with the development of the state apparatus, and was conditioned by the nature of the economy and different modes of military mobilization. Thus, I take this dramatic shift in China’s public financial system striding the Mongol conquest period as the focal point to study the factors that influenced the divergent paths of state formation, as well as the relationship between different kinds of state power and the economy

642410.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
642410.value: The role of the Chinese state in economic development is a major issue in the study of political economy. China's rapid economic change and substantial social transformation during the past three decades has become common knowledge. Much of this progress is accredited to her reform-oriented state power, especially her economic policies that welcome market freedom and embrace foreign investments. From a political economy perspective, China’s reforms can be viewed as a successful transition from a command economy system to a market-based public financial system. What escapes the general public is that this is not the first time a central Chinese government sustained its power based on market expansion. By the eleventh century, the Chinese state was already drawing the majority of tax revenues from the market and developed a cooperative and mutually beneficial relationship with merchants. This Schumpeterian trajectory challenges the usual division between modern and pre-industrial pattern of state power and highlights an important fact in Chinese history that the Chinese state could play an active and crucial role in forming the relationship between the state and the market economy.

642410.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
642410.value: This historical analysis based on Chinese experience tells how the state could be formed to fullfill the objectives identified and shared by the ruling elite. Rather than viewing the state itself as an objective, the making of a state shall be taken as a tool for promoting social welfare and living standards.

642810.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
642810.value: "Anything good in life is either illegal, immoral, or fattening" -- Unknown Despite strong social influences to the contrary, people are often tempted to behave in ways that are normatively unacceptable. Such behaviors may range from inappropriate, such as over-indulgence, to unethical and even downright illegal, such as software piracy. Indeed, it is evident that the proliferation of sub-prime mortgage lending that brought about the current financial crisis was caused by an unhappy confluence of such non-normative behaviors: lenders' willingness to cut corners in search of profits, coupled with consumers' greed in living beyond their means. As recent events (e.g., Madoff, AIG, Enron, Chen Shui-bian) have amply demonstrated, people in positions of responsibility are not averse to such behaviors either. What causes people to behave in such ways? We propose that people's lay theories are important determinants of normatively inappropriate behaviors. Lay theories are basic assumptions that ordinary people hold about themselves and their world (Dweck 1996). They form an integral part of an individual’s belief system, and influence most human judgments and behaviors (Wyer 2004). This research proposes a lay theory prism to examine the mechanisms underlying two types of inappropriate behaviors: cheating and greed. We note that while such behaviors are likely related (e.g., more greed increases cheating), each is important enough in its own right, calling for in-depth exploration. The first part of this research will focus on cheating, and will investigate how an individual’s beliefs whether success is determined by oneself or by external factors influences ethical decision-making. Traditional wisdom holds that a belief in personal responsibility is an important driver of motivation and morality. We suggest that such beliefs, while facilitating ethical behavior in relatively unimportant situations, heighten unethical behavior when people really care about the outcomes of their decisions. In the second part of this research, we propose to investigate lay theories of greed--the belief that people in general are greedy. We suggest that this belief acts as a signal that greed is normatively acceptable, licensing consumers to overextend themselves financially and otherwise. We propose a set of multiple experiments that investigate the motivational underpinnings of these effects, and delineate boundary conditions. Together, these propositions have important implications for marketers and policy-makers alike, for instance, in understanding the causes of the current financial crisis. Theoretically, this research introduces the important construct of lay theories to current understanding of inappropriate behaviors. “生活中的好事物是非法的，不道德的，或致肥的” –未知 雖然社會對一些常態性的不當行為有鉅大的迥響，但人們卻常常表現這些不當的行為。這些不當行為包括過度放縱，不道德，以及非法的行為，如有關盜版軟件行為。事實上，由次級房屋信貸危機演變成的金融危機明顯地是一些不愉快的合流非規範性行為所造成的──貸款人為求賺取更多利潤而走捷徑，而消費者的貪婪也令他們入不敷支。最近的事件﹝如：麥道夫，美國國際集團，安然，陳水扁﹞已充分證明，負責重要崗位的人亦不反對這些非規範性行為。 是什麼原因導致人們有這樣的行為呢？我們認為「常民理論」﹝Lay theories﹞是控制人們的常態性不當行為的重要因素。「常民理論」假設一般人對自己及世界有一套自己的看法﹝Dweck 1996﹞。他們整合個人的信仰體系，並影響大多數人的判斷和行為﹝Wyer 2004﹞。本研究提出一個「常民理論」的棱鏡，探討人們在控制欺騙和貪婪兩種不當行為的機制。我們注意到，雖然這些行為很可能是相關的（例如，更多的貪婪會促使更多的欺詐），但其獨立的重要性亦很值得進一步的深入研究。 第一部分本研究的第一部分將集中在作弊的行為上，並探討由外在因素或內在因素形成的個人信念對倫理決策的影響。傳統觀點認為，個人責任感的信念是驅動著動力和道德觀念。我們認為，個人責任感的信念在不重要的事情上促進道德行為，反之，在重要的事情上增加其不道德的行為。本研究的第二部分將探討「常民理論」應用在貪婪的理論上──一般人也是貪婪的。我們認為，這一個信念令貪婪被視為常態性接受的信號，也令消費者心態上許可其在經濟上和其他範圍上的盲目揮霍。我們提出了多項實驗，作為研究推動這些信念的基礎，並勾畫出這些信念的邊界和條件。 總括，這些主張對市場營銷和政策制定者有重要意義，例如，應用在理解現時的金融危機上。本研究也透過「常民理論」去理解和建構不當行為的理論。

642810.label: Realisation of objectives
642810.value: Till the last progress report, we had focused on writing up and resubmitting the ethics paper, and running experiments on the greed and non-normative behaviors fronts. The greatest breakthrough was the collaboration with a local business that allowed us to run a year-long field experiment on-site (leading to multiple papers, one of which has been accepted at the ACR conference in October 2013), and the greatest successes were papers published in Psychological Science (the premier empirical journal in psychology) and the Journal of Consumer Research (JCR). Subsequently, we have a revise and resubmit request at JCR, and a manuscript currently being rewritten (after being rejected at Psychological Science) targeted at Management Science. The single greatest obstruction, as detailed in the previous report, was that the ethics paper had been "scooped" by Lammers et al. (2010). This paper was published after the current proposal had been submitted and approved, and was under scrutiny for possible retraction. We have nevertheless persisted in developing the idea and trying to get it published, since the feedback has been that the basic idea as hypothesized was indeed publishable. To summarize, we believe that the objectives have not been fully realized on the ethics part of the project, but have been more than 100% achieved on the greed part. The PI is currently also working on several extensions of the greed part of the project (e.g., the aforementioned field experiment), which have been funded by GRF HKUST 692413.

642810.label: Major findings and research outcome
642810.value: We find that people's lay beliefs do indeed have significant and enduring effects on their non-normative behavior. These findings hold across the domains of ethical behavior, greed-related behaviors such as obesity and resource-sharing, and need for uniqueness vs. conformity. The following papers have been published and/or submitted based on this project: 1. McFerran, Brent and Anirban Mukhopadhyay (2013), “Lay Theories of Obesity Predict Actual Body Mass,” Psychological Science, 24, 8 (August), 1428-1436. This paper shows that people's lay theories about the causes of obesity systematically influence their own overeating and therefore body mass. 2. Chan, Elaine, Jaideep Sengupta, and Anirban Mukhopadhyay (2013), “The Antecedents of Anticipatory Purchase: Reconciling the Two Routes to Optimism,” Journal of Consumer Psychology, 23, 1 (January), 90-105. This paper shows that people's lay theories regarding optimism can lead them to buy products that they cannot even use. 3. Wang, Chen and Anirban Mukhopadhyay (2012), “The Dynamics of Goal Revision: A Cybernetic Multi-Period Test-Operate-Test-Adjust-Loop (TOTAL) Model of Self-Regulation,” Journal of Consumer Research, 38, 5 (February), 815-833. This paper presents a mathematical model of how people update their normatively desired goals based on past success or failure. 4. 642810.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
642810.value: Despite strong social influences to the contrary, people are often tempted to behave in ways that are normatively unacceptable. Such behaviors may range from inappropriate, such as nonconformity, or over-indulgence leading to obesity, to unethical and even downright illegal, such as software piracy. What causes people to behave in such ways? We propose that people's lay theories are important determinants of normatively inappropriate behaviors. Lay theories are basic assumptions that ordinary people hold about themselves and their world (Dweck 1996). They form an integral part of an individual’s belief system, and influence most human judgments and behaviors (Wyer 2004). This research proposes a lay theory prism to examine the mechanisms underlying inappropriate behaviors. Multiple papers stemming from this project address these issues in different ways, all studying greed, obesity, resource-sharing, conformity, and other such instantiations of non-normative behavior. For example, one published paper demonstrates that peoples lay beliefs about the cause of obesity influence their own body mass indices -- this research was conducted in Hong Kong, South Korea, the US, and Canada, and has received widespread media attention including in the South China Morning Post. Theoretically, this research introduces the important construct of lay theories to current understanding of inappropriate behaviors.

643010.label: Project Title(Chinese)
643010.value: 資訊不確定性下的管理決策、實質盈餘管理、與財務報告品質

643010.label: Project Objectives
643010.value: To investigate managers' willingness to engage in opportunistic decisions to reduce discretionary spending, in contrast to similar decisions that are optimal responses to unexpected increases in uncertainty. To investigate the effect of exogenous uncertainty shocks on managers' willingness to manage earnings. To examine the potential impact of exogenous uncertainty shock on the choice between real and accrual manipulation.
rows: To investigate managers' willingness to engage in opportunistic decisions to reduce discretionary spending, in contrast to similar decisions that are optimal responses to unexpected increases in uncertainty.
To investigate the effect of exogenous uncertainty shocks on managers' willingness to manage earnings.
To examine the potential impact of exogenous uncertainty shock on the choice between real and accrual manipulation.

643010.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
643010.value: When companies face economic difficulties, managers often respond by cutting investment and discretionary spending such as advertising and research and development. Traditionally, this behavior has been viewed as falling under the rubric of real earnings manipulation, with the implication that managers opportunistically distort business decisions by deviating from the optimum. Recent evidence in economics, however, suggests that the managerial decision to cut spending may be an optimal reaction to an unexpected increase in the uncertainty inherent in the business environment. In this study we use several measures of uncertainty to distinguish the settings where managers behave opportunistically from the ones where managerial decisions are optimal conditional on the information available to them. We show that situations characterized by information asymmetry, where insiders (managers) have access to better information than outsiders (investors), have different implications for both groups than the situations characterized by uncertainty, where neither group is better informed than the other. We also investigate the effect of information uncertainty on the managers’ incentives to engage in real, in contrast to accrual-based, earnings management, and the effect of managerial decisions on the accrual-based measures of financial reporting quality that are widely used in the literature. 當公司面臨經濟困難時，經理人的因應方法通常是裁減投資支出和廣告及研發費用等裁決性支出。傳統上此一行為被視為屬於以實質經濟活動操縱盈餘，亦即經理人偏離了最適情況，投機地扭曲了企業決策。然而，近來經濟學上的證據顯示經理人裁減支出的決策，可能正是對企業環境中意外增加的不確定性所做出的最佳反應。本研究以數種衡量指標來區分（一）經理人的投機行為及（二）經理人基於既有資訊所做出的最適決策。我們說明在會計上，資訊不對稱（即內部經理人比外部投資者有更多資訊）和不確定性（即任一方都不比另一方有更多資訊）有不同的含意。我們進一步研究資訊不確定性對經理人選擇實質或帳面盈餘管理的動機之影響。同時，文獻上廣泛使用以應計基礎指標來衡量財務報表品質，我們也研究管理決策是否影響這些衡量指標。

643010.label: Realisation of objectives
643010.value: The project has led to an empirical observation that we had not anticipated at the time we wrote the application: that the nature of uncertainty—i.e., whether or not all possible outcomes and their precise probabilities are known at the beginning of the problem—has important implications for the optimal decision strategy and, consequently, for the properties of accounting information. The realization that the type of uncertainty matters, and that the accounting literature to date has largely ignored the implications of “radical” uncertainty (i.e., uncertainty where all possible outcomes are not known), had two consequences: we had to review the sizeable literatures on radical uncertainty published in decision analysis, economics, management, and finance. In the process, we have discovered one reason why most research papers studying radical uncertainty report results of either pure theoretical analysis or laboratory experiments: to date, there are no reliable measures of radical uncertainty based on archival data. As a result, the success of the publication is, to a large extent, determined by the authors’ ability to convince the editor and the reviewers that their measure makes sense. For example, Armstrong et al. (2009) infer radical uncertainty from the divergence of opinions of professional forecasters. This method only allows to measure uncertainty can only be measured at the level of the economy as a whole. But a large management literature (which we review in the paper) documents that managers’ perceptions of uncertainty differ markedly even if the mangers are working in the same firm. Accordingly, in our paper, we propose a firm-specific measure that relies upon the revealed preference argument and a substantial theoretical and empirical literature studying corporate response to unanticipated increases in uncertainty (Bloom 2009 provides an excellent review). Although our measure has received approval in the workshops, referees have been skeptical. Our task is to better explain the underlying logic and allay the concerns about potential alternative explanations.

643010.label: Major findings and research outcome
643010.value: 1. Radical uncertainty serves as the simplest explanation of the enduring presence of accounting conservatism in practice. The literature studying accounting conservatism has grown at a steady pace over the past two decades, yet the theoretical explanation remains elusive: as has been pointed out by several authors, the practice—which involves distorting reported information so that the information conveying good news is deliberately delayed—is difficult to explain within the received contracting framework. The decision-theoretic explanation that we propose is free from this criticism. We build upon the latest advances in the theory of unawareness (at the time of our writing, the two key references were still in press). The paper was rejected by Journal of Accounting Research on the grounds that it “adds little theoretically.” Our interpretation is that, because the theory is, indeed, very new, the reviewer is simply not familiar with it. We have updated the paper based on the comments and submitted an updated version to Accounting, Organizations & Society, where it is currently under review. 2. Firms characterized by high responsiveness to unanticipated changes in the environment—we dub them “alert” firms—have an advantage over “inert” firms in uncertain times, but incur additional costs in relatively calm times. After reviewing sizeable literatures in management, psychology, and biology, we have written a second paper demonstrating that alert firms exhibit the characteristics predicted by the theory. Although the paper was rejected by Management Science, The associate editor wrote: “In summary my opinion was that the idea and concept behind the paper was excellent. I learned a lot from this and will likely cite the paper in future.” The primary concerns of the reviewers had to do with our empirical proxy for alertness that we used. After consultation with a senior faculty member in the Management Department, we decided to submit the current version of the paper to the Journal of Economics & Management Strategy, where it is currently under review. We have presented an earlier version of the paper at the Annual Meeting of the American Accounting Association and at several universities in Hong Kong, Europe, and the U.S.

643010.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
643010.value: Based on the feedback from workshops, referees, and editors, we view both research questions that emerged as a result of our investigation as worth pursuing further, most likely in the form of purely theoretical investigations. This would require a substantial time commitment on the part of the principal investigator, who is currently involved in several projects.

643010.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
643010.value: When firms (or individuals) face known risks, the standard tools (such as insurance, hedging, and risk management) can be used to reduce or eliminate them. The situation is altogether different when the nature of potential problems is unknown: they can be brought about unanticipated and thus surprising actions by competitors and governments, political and technological developments, and changes in consumers’ tastes. In short, future is unknowable because it is yet to be created. In our project, we address the question: “What is the decision maker’s optimal strategy in the face of radical uncertainty?” The answer is: to be prudent (or cautious), i.e., put more weight on negative than on positive outcomes in computing the expected results from proposed actions. Surprisingly, constantly scanning the environment for subtle signs of unanticipated developments is not always an optimal strategy: it turns out that it is optimal for the majority of the population (of the firms) to remain “inert,” i.e., unaware of the new developments, until definitive information becomes available.

643310.value: 零售競爭下的供應鏈合約及顧客替代購物行為

643310.label: Project Objectives
643310.value: To study the contract design problem of a manufacturer under non-discriminating contracting regime, and the impact of non-discriminating contracting on the manufacturer, the retail market and the consumers. To develop a theoretical rationale to better understand how the existence of competing retail outlets affects customers' price responsiveness and their substitution behavior, and to provide insights into how a manufacturer may design contracts with retailers to induce desired market conditions and consumer behavior. To examine the impact of a manufacturer on retail competition and on consumer welfare, and gain insights into the role of public policy in regulating business conduct affecting retail competition.

To develop a theoretical rationale to better understand how the existence of competing retail outlets affects customers' price responsiveness and their substitution behavior, and to provide insights into how a manufacturer may design contracts with retailers to induce desired market conditions and consumer behavior.

643310.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
643310.value: Many manufacturers sell their products through various competing retailers in the same market. Due to legal issues or other constraints such as fairness, some manufacturers may provide different buyers with non-discriminating contracts. For example, the Robinson-Patman Act forbids companies from selling to different retailers at discriminating prices in the United States. Hong Kong has been working on a cross-sector Competition Bill that sanctions anti-competitive conduct. How a manufacturer contracts with competing retailers under non-discrimination constraints is an important problem. Note that by contracting with competing retailers, manufacturers should be aware of how competition among retailers affects consumer choice/substituion behavior, which in turn influences retailers' equilibrium solutions and thus the manufacturer's contracting decisions. We propose to consider the contracting problem under non-discrimination constraints and focus on the effects of customer substitution behavior on retailer competition and the manufacturer's resulting contracting strategy. We will first study how customer substitution among different retailers impacts retailers' equilibrium procurement decisions and discuss the implications that non-discrimination constraints may generate. We will then examine the manufacturer's decision about whether he should sell to competing retailers when he has no flexibility to differentiate them by offering different contracts. We will investigate the preference of a manufacturer for monopolistic or competitive retail markets and how this preference is influenced by customer substitution behavior, production cost and types of contracts (e.g., wholesale price, buyback price and sales rebate). We will further study the impact of direct sales (i.e., the manufacturer sells its product directly to customers) on the customers' purchasing behavior and competition with existing retailers if any. Finally, we will look at the social impact of such contracting problems and the role of public policy in regulating retail competition. The successful completion of the project will contribute to incorporating customer behavior into supply chain management. Particularly, it will improve our understanding of how customer choice/substitution behavior affects retail competition and thus the manufacturer's contracting strategy. 許多生產商通過同一市場裏的多個互相競爭的零售商出售產品。由於法律約束及其他如公平因素等考慮，一些生產商會向不同的零售商提供非區別性的合約。例如，美國的罗宾逊一帕特曼法禁止公司利用區別性的價格把貨品賣給不同零售商，香港亦考慮實施跨行業競爭法。在非區別性合約的框架下，生產商怎樣與互相競爭的零售商制定合法是一個重要課題。當與互相競爭的零售商制定合法時，生產商亦須意識到零售商的互相競爭會怎樣影響到消費者的選擇及替代行為，這亦影響到零售商的采購均衡解及生產商的合約決定。 我們建議考慮非區別性框架下的合約問題，並集中於顧客替代行為對於零售競爭及生產商合約策略的影響。我們首先研究顧客替代行為怎樣影響零售商的採購決定及討論非區別性框架所產生的效果。我們然後會探討當生產商不能利用不同合約區別不同零售商時會否售予互相競爭的零售商的決定。我們還計劃探討生產商對獨佔性的及競爭性的零售市場的偏好，及這偏好如何受顧客替代行為、生產成本及合約種類所影響。我們還將進一步研究直銷對顧客購買行為及與現有零售商的競爭的影響。最後，我們會探討這個合約問題的社會影響及公共政策在調整零售競爭的角色。我們預計項目的成功完成會對於包含顧客行為的供應鏈管理作出貢獻，亦會對顧客的選擇及替代行為怎樣影響零售競爭及生產商的合約策略有更多的了解。

643310.label: Realisation of objectives
643310.value: We consider two problems in this research problem. In the first problem, we focus on the case when the supplier either offers the same return contract or the same linear rebate contract to both retailers. We study the supplier's optimal contracting decisions. We show that it is never optimal for the supplier to offer a moderate wholesale price such that the high-price retailer orders more than its highest possible primary demand. The supplier's optimal strategy is to offer either a high wholesale price such that only the high-price retailer stocks the product or a low wholesale price such that demand overflow is possible in both directions. Which one is optimal depends ultimately on the price difference between the two retailers. We show that it is more likely for the supplier to sell to only the high-price retailer under return contracts, and sell to both retailers under rebate contracts. The reason is that return (rebate) contracts enlarge (reduce) the asymmetry between retailers which increases (reduces) the incentive of the supplier to sell only to the high-price retailer. The first problem led us to consider the idea of cost reduction, to consider the impact of customer behavior. In the second problem, we consider a novel model in which a firm’s later production cost may be reduced due to both production learning and technology advancement, but the magnitude of cost reduction is uncertain before production starts. This uncertainty in the magnitude of cost reduction leads to uncertainty in the firm’s future production cost. Depending on the pricing strategy, the firm may decide to set the later price in response to the realized cost reduction (for example, under dynamic pricing). Thus, at the beginning of the selling season, the firm faces uncertainty in future cost and customers may also face uncertainty in future price. The firm decides the pricing strategy and strategic customers decide when to purchase under these uncertainties. We consider the impact of production learning and technology advancement on prices, quantities and the firm’s profit.

643310.label: Major findings and research outcome
643310.value: In the first problem, we also characterize supplier's optimal choice between return and rebate contracts. In the case of a supplier selling to a single newsvendor, it is a well-known result that rebate contract can never be optimal. The reason is behind that, a return contract can coordinate the supply chain with any profit allocation and a rebate contract can coordinate the supply chain only when the supplier's profit is negative. On the contrary, we show that it can be optimal for the supplier to offer a rebate contract when selling to two heterogeneous newsvendor. In particular, it is optimal for the supplier to offer a return contract when the retail price difference is either high or low, and a rebate contract when the retail price difference is moderate. When the retail price difference is small, the supplier can use a return contract to achieve high supply chain efficiency and capture most profits as well. When the retail price difference is moderate, it is impossible to achieve these two goals under a return contract; instead the supplier should use a linear sales rebate contract to reduce the asymmetry between the two retailers. When the price difference is large, a return contract dominates again because the supplier sells only to the high-price retailer. For the second problem, we first consider the case in which the firm uses a dynamic pricing strategy. Even though dynamic pricing is common in practice and provides the firm with a high degree of flexibility to change prices, it also provides incentives for customers to wait. Thus, we also study two other pricing strategies, namely, price commitment and price matching. Under price commitment, the firm commits to a pre-announced future price. Under price matching, customers who purchase before a price cut (if there is any) are fully reimbursed the difference. We show that in general the firm’s profit is higher when future cost is more uncertain, but not necessarily when cost reduction is more significant. In addition, production learning and technology advancement can have opposite effects on the optimal pricing decisions and the choice of pricing strategy.

643310.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
643310.value: This project shows that the choice of contract is affected hugely by the non-discriminating contracting regime. While the results in this project shed some light on the contract design problem in this context, it would be interesting to consider more complicated settings and more contract types. Our results also suggest that interaction between cost reduction and strategic customer behavior are important considerations in a firm's pricing decisions. Definitely, this will also be another interesting direction for future research

643310.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
643310.value: Results from this research project contribute to existing literature in two important directions. First, it shows that non-discriminating contracting regime leads to different choice of contract when a supplier sells to competing retailers. This suggests that practitioners and academicians need to rethink contract design problems. Second, our results also brings in a new component of cost reduction to the research of strategic customer behavior, which we believe, has paved a good direction for fruitful research for researchers in this area.

643410.label: Project Objectives
643410.value: a) The core assumptions of the theory Asian values will be subjected to a rigorous study, i.e., whether citizens in eight Asian societies have greater stress on the value of obedience, order, family, and respect for authority than citizens in thirty-one Western countries, and whether greater attachment to those values decreases mass support for democracy. The neglected public conceptions of democracy, institutional legacy, mass values and perceived performance will be included in more comprehensive causal models to explain mass support for democracy among eight Asian and thirty-one Western societies. The data have been extracted from the latest World Values Survey gathered from a standard questionnaire administered globally between 2005 and 2008. b) The relative explanatory power of different variables or categories of variables across the thirty-nine societies will be explored. Analysis will seek some common, powerful explanatory factors among Asian and/or Western societies that account for mass support for democracy. c) While my research will focus on whether the Asian values deter unqualified support for democracy, it will also whether those Asian values affect popular conceptions of democracy, and whether different conceptiions affect support for democracy. d) I propose a 2-year study to put the theory of Asian values to a more rigorous investigation and disseminate research findings through journal publications (e.g., Comparative Politics, Comparative Political Studies, British Journal of Political Science) and conference papers. Long-term Impact: a) This research will unravel whether Asian values are incompatible with mass support for electoral, liberal or social democracy. The findings will contribute to the theoretical debate about Asian values. The project will also help us assess the facilitating and constraining conditions on establishing democratic systems in Asia, a region with rising economic and political clout in the world today. b) The research will uncover whether certain social groups have different levels of support for democracy. It will inform us of any underlying political tensions among social groups over democracy in various societies, which can be politically and economically destabilizing. c) The proposed research, based on the World Values Survey, will generate empirical results which can advance longitudinal research useful for understanding long-term democratic development in Asia and the West.

643410.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
643410.value: Abstract of Research: Proponents of the theory of Asian values argue that i.) Asians lay more emphasis on the value of obedience and respect for authority than Westerners, and that ii.) those values decrease mass support for Western-style democracy, thereby obstructing democratic development in Asia (Dalton & Ong, 2006). My proposed research has four features that puts the theory of Asian values to a more rigorous test: i.) attention to public conceptions of democracy, and ii.) inclusion of additional countries, iii.) of more explanatory and control variables, and iv.) of more indicators of Asian values. 1. Previous empirical research of the theory of Asian values has examined whether Asians place greater emphasis on obedience and respect for authority, and less on democracy than Westerners (Diamond, 2008). Whether greater emphasis on obedience and respect for authorities decreases individuals’ support for democracy has also been studied (Dalton & Ong, 2006). Those research, however, neglected how respondents conceived democracy, and ignored some respondents having conceived of pseudo-democracy as genuine democracy, thereby inflating the actual level of support for democracy. My research includes only those respondents who conceive of democracy as involving one or more of the three major manifestations of Western-style democracy - electoral, liberal, or social democracy for accurately examining: i) how strongly Asians emphasis obedience, family, order and respect for authority; ii) how those Asian values affect popular understanding of democracy; and iii) whether the values deter support for democracy. 2. Much previous research included no or very few Western countries in testing the theory of Asian values. This research proposes to use comparable data from eight Asian and thirty-one Western societies to test the theory more rigorously (Table 1). 3. In testing the causal efficacy of the value of obedience and respect for authority in explaining mass support for democracy, previous studies have ignored the sub-type of authoritarian regime as a competing explanatory variable. Authoritarian regimes with a greater legacy of military rule and competitive authoritarianism are more likely to collapse or democratize respectively (Brownlee, 2009). The two sub-types of authoritarian regimes may trigger more support for democracy than other sub-types, and will be included in testing the theory of Asian values. Other variables concerning values, perceived performance, and socio-demographic factors are included too to test the theory. 4. Besides measuring individuals’obedience and respect for authority, this research assesses their emphasis on family and order, as additional constituents of the Asian values. 亞洲價值理論的支持者認為：1）亞洲人比西方人更加重視服從和對權威的尊重；2）這些價值觀降低了西方式民主的群眾支持，從而阻礙了亞洲的民主發展 (Dalton & Ong, 2006)。我的研究提案將對亞洲價值理論進行更為嚴格的檢驗，具有如下四個特點：a)關注公眾對民主這一概念的理解，b）列入更多的國家，c）更多的解釋與控制變量，以及d）更多關於亞洲價值的測量指標。

643410.label: Realisation of objectives
643410.value: One major challenge has been that when all the original proposed 43 countries, which include both democratic and non-democratic countries, are included in analysis, because of their sharply divergent nature, no theoretically meaningful and consistently significant explanatory factors can be found. To overcome this, instead of using data of 43 countries from the World Values Survey, all the authoritarian countries in that dataset, which comprises 16 nation-states, are included in the sample. After this treatment, theoretically meaningful and statistically significant causes are found. Another challenge is that Asian values are not found significant in the statistical tests. Therefore, the research has shifted its focus on testing the causal efficacy of variables in collective learning, i.e., education, liberal conception of democracy, and legacy of non-democratic regimes. Using data of over a dozen authoritarian countries collected from World Values Survey between 2005 and 2008, this study finds that variables of collective learning, i.e., education, liberal conception of democracy, and legacy of non-democratic regimes, do shape democratic support. However, the variables of Asian values do not matter for support for democracy. With a multi-level model, those three collective learning variables are found important in explaining the support after controlling cultural and structural factors. More specifically, more education and a greater liberal conception of democracy triggers more support for democracy. Also, the longer a country has been ruled by a one-party system or military rule, the lesser the public support for democracy. Lastly, the research shows a liberal understanding of democracy interacts with education and economic development in conditioning democratic support. The research concludes that a liberal conception of democracy and the legacy of authoritarian regime, both reflecting citizens’ collective learning, have been pivotal and yet neglected factors to explain democratic support in authoritarian regimes.

643410.label: Major findings and research outcome
643410.value: 1. Using the latest dataset of World Values Survey and focusing on more than a dozen countries, the research shows some ﬁndings cohering well with the literature: a higher interest in politics will unsurprisingly raise support for democracy. Also, perceived economic performance, as testified in much research, plays a prominent role in accounting for democratic support. 2. This study diverges significantly from the existing literature in some aspects. This investigation demonstrates the causal efficacy of collective learning variables for explaining democratic support, including the pivotal one of liberal conception of democracy. 3. While the past literature has rarely provided quantitative confirmation of the impact of conception of democracy on support across societies, this research provides a pioneering quantitative confirmation that liberal understanding of democracy can robustly explain democratic support under different models of sixteen authoritarian countries. 4. Another crucial collective learning variable found casually relevant for explaining democratic support has been education. This finding entails the presence of an important social base of social resistance to authoritarianism and public dedication to democracy. 5. Still another original finding pertains to the repercussion of regime legacy of authoritarianism. Existing research already shows institutional or regime effects unfold over time, sometimes a long time, and the temporal effects are cumulative (Brownlee, 2007; Collier & Collier, 1991; Hite and Cesarini, 2004; Mahoney, 2002; Gerring et. al. 2011). This research finds the total duration of authoritarian regimes as relevant to account for the support. The variable has illuminated the effect of cumulative and collective learning about legacies of regime types on democratic support. Respondents’ support of democracy do not only rest on their educational background or understanding of democracy, but also on the duration of authoritarian regimes. This result evinces a strong, long-term impact of regime legacies on collective learning, which eventually impinge on democratic support. 6. Overall speaking, variables of collective learning, including education, conception of democracy, and regime legacy of authoritarian rule are the most important explanatory factors for democratic support among individual and macro-level variables. Without the need to use specific national histories of over a dozen countries to account for their democratic support, the causal efficacy of the duration of the past dominant authoritarian regimes suggests the theoretical potential of duration of national legacies. Citizens living in countries with different duration of authoritarian legacies have reacted distinctively in terms of democratic support.

643410.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
643410.value: Theoretically, given the importance of the liberal conception in accounting for the support, future research needs to unravel the determinants of the liberal understanding of democracy. This is especially the case since it may be relatively easier to change the conception of democracy than the duration of authoritarian legacy. Of no less importance, as electoral democracy and social democracy are other genuine forms of democracy, it is theoretically relevant to explore the presence and possible causal effect of an “electoral” or “social” conception of democracy in future. Lastly, the sample of this research is confined to sixteen authoritarian countries spanning from 2005 to 2008 with different degrees of authoritarianism. To assess the generalizability of findings for other cultural and structural settings, further research is warranted to understand how individual and national differences may condition democratic support in a larger sample of authoritarian regimes. It would be meaningful to test various models used here in other authoritarian regimes in future, should the data become available.

643510.label: Project Objectives
643510.value: To understand the cross-level, bottom-up effects of firms' network and learning strategies on cluster-level heterogeneity in terms of emergent network structure, knowledge flows, and new knowledge creation. To understand the cross-level, top-down effects of clusters' network structure and knowledge flows on cluster firms’ innovative performance. To gain insights into how a firm's network relationships and knowledge stocks influence net benefits received from locating in different types of clusters by examining the joint effects of firm and cluster characteristics on firm innovative performance. To gain insights and practical knowledge about how a firm’s location decisions affect its innovative performance and how government policy can more effectively promote innovation in clusters by influencing their composition and creating particular opportunities for networking and knowledge sharing. Hence, we aim to disseminate our findings to entrepreneurs and policymakers in Hong Kong and elsewhere, who are interested in learning about how clusters can be promoted to support regional innovative activities.

643510.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
643510.value: Take any industry and one will observe that its innovative activities are highly concentrated in a few geographic “hot spots.” Prominent examples are software development in India, leather fashion in Italy, and financial services in Hong Kong. Recent research highlights the key role of localized networks in facilitating the creation and transfer of “tacit knowledge,” which flows less freely across large geographic distance and hence constitutes a strategic firm resource. Yet while the idea that clusters are hotbeds of innovation is compelling, we still know little about the emergence of structure and innovation in clusters, how a cluster’s innovativeness can be sustained over time, and when firms benefit from locating in a cluster. Casual observation and recent research suggest that clusters with similar endowments exhibit diverse evolutionary trajectories, with some clusters and firms thriving and others struggling to survive. It is therefore important to understand the processes by which innovative clusters emerge and how firms can extract more value from cluster membership. We aim to generate new theoretical insights and practical knowledge about how spatial clustering generates both collective and individual advantage through a unique multimethod research. The proposed study will combine agent-based simulation modeling of cluster networks and knowledge flows with an empirical investigation of the effects of these emergent cluster characteristics on innovation among firms in the nanotechnology industry. Previous research has often assumed the existence of localized networks and knowledge flows without considering structural differences across clusters and the possibility that firms asymmetrically benefit from cluster membership. Our simulation approach will enable us to generate novel hypotheses about how the individual network and learning strategies of firms aggregate into collective outcomes in terms of emergent network structure, knowledge flows, and innovation. The key advantage of the simulation is that we can directly measure tacit knowledge flows and track complex cluster dynamics across multiple clusters over long periods of time. To cross-validate and extend the simulation results, we will also conduct an empirical investigation of firms operating in different regional clusters in the U.S. nanotechnology industry. This promising new technological field has witnessed rapid growth and exhibits significant geographic concentration. Our empirical study will examine inter-cluster differences in terms of the structure of organizational, inventor and patent citation linkages, and then consider how firms with different types of network connections and knowledge bases differentially benefit from locating in these nanotechnology clusters in terms of their publication and patenting rates. 我們經常發現產業創新活動高度集中在某些區域性的“熱點”，比如，軟件發展在印度，皮革時裝在意大利，金融服務在香港。但是，雖然區域聚類是創新溫床的觀點很吸引人，對於聚類中創新的產生，維持以及哪些企業從聚類中得益，我們都不是很清楚。運用獨特的多層次分析方法，我們的研究意在提供理解區域聚類如何讓個體和群體受益的理論和實用知識。我們的提項將同時使用模擬模型和實證模型來驗證納米技術產業中區域聚類和創新的關係。現有的研究一般在考慮局部性的網絡和知識流動時，假定它們的存在是沒有結構差別的，也不考慮企業從聚類中的得益是否相同。模擬模型的長處是我們可以直接衡量在長時間內各個聚類中的知識流動和網絡變化。為了進一步驗證和發展模樣模型的結果，我們將實證調查分析美國納米技術產業公司在不同區域聚類的狀況。我們的實證研究將分析調查在不同聚類中那些企業網絡和知識流動的差別，同時也考慮有著不同網絡連接和不同知識基本結構的企業如何在這些聚類中有不同的益處。

643510.label: Realisation of objectives
643510.value: On 7 September 2011, the chief Co-I for this project (Prof. Max Boisot) unexpectedly died. As a consequence of this tragedy, the project could not achieve its intended objectives because Prof. Boisot's knowledge was of fundamental importance to the project. After his death, we tried to find replacement for his contribution but unfortunately this did not work out well. During 2012-2103 some new programmers were attracted to work together with Dr. Martin Ihrig (who is an adjunct faculty at Wharton) to further develop and validate the prototype simulation model. However, due to some turnover caused by programmers leaving to pursue other opportunities, the progress made was less than anticipated. Some new features have been added to the simulation and the model was further validated by comparing its results to some existing real-world datasets that were collected by Wharton faculty in recent years. At HKUST, the research assistant has been helping the PI with further assembling a dataset of networks and knowledge flows among firms operating in the nanotechnology industry. Data collection turned out to be more time-consuming than expected, however, such that more time is needed to analyze the data and writing up the results. ￼￼

643510.label: Major findings and research outcome
643510.value: Our project demonstrates through agent-based simulation modelling how a cluster’s configuration in terms of individual firms’ learning and network strategies affects the endogenous emergence of network structure, knowledge flows, and innovation. Combining Boisot’s (1995, 1998) work on the Information Space (I-Space) with recent research on networks and social capital (Ibarra, Kilduff, & Tsai, 2005), we juxtapose two types of learning strategies (hoarding vs. sharing strategies) with two types of network strategies (bonding vs bridging strategies) to yield four distinct cluster configurations. Our research helps to better understand what configuration of strategies may enhance cluster-level knowledge knowledge spillovers and which firms disproportionately contribute to, and benefit from, this public good. Relatively greater levels of knowledge sharing and network bonding can be expected to increase cluster-level knowledge creation due to enhanced connectivity and spillovers (Fleming et al., 2007). However, an alternative argument would be that greater sharing and cohesion eliminates diversity such that clusters also require firms that hoard knowledge and forge extracluster ties (Arikan, 2009). The results from our simulation suggest that cluster innovation is most strongly influenced by the learning strategies of those firms that occupy bridging positions in the cluster's network structure. That is, it matters most whether firms that are linked to otherwise unconnected cluster firms pursue hoarding or sharing strategies. Interesting, when there is a mix of both strategies present, innovation at the cluster level is higher than when the cluster is dominated by firms pursuing only one type of learning strategy. This importance of learning strategy diversity only applies to firms occupying bridging positions in the cluster network. For firms situated in peripheral positions, innovation mainly depends on the relatedness of their knowledge assets to those of other firms in the cluster network.

643510.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
643510.value: The simulation we have developed so far yields a number of opportunities for further research. First, future work could collect empirical data to yield new insights into how cluster characteristics in terms of network structure and patterns of knowledge flows affect innovation and performance among firms in different types of clusters. Our simulation results suggest that the patterning of interactions and knowledge sharing in clusters creates important heterogeneity across firms located in a particular cluster. Naturaly, further research is necessary to validate and extend these insights. Second, future work could examine how individual firm characteristics in terms of network position and knowledge stocks amplify the performance effects of cluster characteristics. In our simulation model, firms pursue distinct networking and learning strategies and preliminary results suggest that the payoff of these strategies depends on characteristics of the overall cluster. Further research is needed that validates and extends these insights by collecting empirical data on the strategies and performance of firms located in different clusters.

643510.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
643510.value: Despite today’s globalizing economy, the importance of spatial clustering of economic activities for the competitive advantage of firms and industries is increasingly noted by economic geographers, sociologists, and management scholars. Clusters, defined as geographic concentrations of interconnected companies and institutions in a particular field, are typical in many industries ranging from movie production in Hollywood and biotechnology in Silicon Valley to software development in India and watch making in Hong Kong. Research on clusters seeks to understand why agglomerations exist, what makes some clusters more or less innovative, and how cluster membership influences firm performance. The current research combines agent-based simulation modelling of network and knowledge flow dynamics in clusters with an empirical investigation of the performance effects of these emergent cluster characteristics. Specifically, the simulation aims to enhance understanding of how inter-cluster differences in terms of network structure, knowledge flows, and innovation endogenously emerge and which firms disproportionately contribute most to these processes. Furthermore, we conduct an empirical study of networks, knowledge flows, and innovation among firms operating in the nanotechnology industry. The empirical study generates theoretical and practical knowledge about the contingent value of spatial clustering by examining what network and learning strategies excel in what types of clusters.

643610.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
643610.value: Multinational corporations (MNCs) are a very complex entity composed of a group of geographically dispersed and goal disparate foreign subsidiaries and parent company headquarters that manage these foreign subsidiaries. Because of geographical as well as cultural distance between parent company headquarters and foreign subsidiaries, understanding how MNCs manage these foreign subsidiaries has been a very pertinent and challenging issue for scholars who are interested in international strategy as well as for practicing managers. In particular, for many MNCs (such as multinational hotel chains), implementing formal organizational structures to control foreign subsidiaries has proven to be rather difficult. For instance, Kostova and Roth (2003: 297) noted that “both research and business practice has provided ample evidence for the limited capacity of formal structures and mechanisms to control and coordinate foreign activities.” Recognizing this limitation, the use of expatriate managers has been identified as another mechanism through which MNCs can exert control over their subsidiaries (Gong, 2003). Thus, expatriate managers act as liaison between the parent company headquarters and host country nationals (HCNs) working in the foreign subsidiaries. However, neither international staffing nor multinational control literature has investigated the impact that different types of MNC and expatriate managers’ control over the foreign subsidiaries have on host country nationals and other relevant stakeholders. For instance, virtually no study thus far has examined the impact of different types of control mechanisms (i.e., input, behavior/process, and output) utilized by expatriate managers on HCNs who work at these foreign subsidiaries, although HCNs are considered to be a vital asset to the MNCs for various reasons. By integrate organizational control literature and recognizing that the MNCs try to control the behaviors of expatriate managers who typically head the foreign subsidiaries while expatriate managers themselves try to control HCNs working in these subsidiaries, we contribute new insights and theoretical perspectives heretofore unexamined in the expatriate or international staffing literature. More specifically, we develop theoretical rationale for the use of different types of control used by the expatriate managers on the host country national subordinates as well as the moderating effect of MNC controls used on expatriate managers on the relationship between expatriate managers’ control behavior and HCN outcomes (such as their satisfaction with the job or performance at work). By so doing, this project has the potential to provide novel insights into the impact of organizational control on MNC stakeholders. 跨國公司是一個非常複雜的組織。她們由很多目標和所在地不同的子公司和負責管理的母公司總部組成，因此她們在地理和文化上都存在差距。這些差異，讓跨國公司中的母公司如何管理她們的子公司成為研究國際戰略的學者和實務經理感興趣的課題。有研究證明，利用正式的組織結構以控制海外子公司(特別是中港跨國公司)是相當困難的。例如，Kostova 和Roth (2003: 297)指出，不同的研究和企業實務提供了充足的證據證明正式結構和機制只有有限能力去控制和協調海外活動。基於這局限，聘用駐海外經理則被認定為另一種控制海外子公司的機制（Gong, 2003）。因此，駐海外經理成為了母公司總部和當地子公司人員的聯繫橋樑。然而，對不同類型的跨國公司和駐海外經理所用的控制手段如何對當地子公司人員和其他持份者所產生的影響是現時的研究所缺乏的。 舉例來說，迄今幾乎沒有文獻研究過駐海外經理用以控制在子公司工作的當地人員所用的控制機制（即輸入，行為 /處理和輸出）。然而當地人員卻被認為是跨國公司的重要資產。例如，他們有本地市場、商業慣例和文化偏好的知識，亦因如此，他們擔當了跨國公司和當地的重要橋樑。他們可以幫助跨國公司克服在海外的責任，並取得當地知識網絡。他們同時有著語言優勢，成本較低，亦不受政府任何可能對輸入海外員工所作的管制。因此，他們是當地未來的管理人才。此外，雖然跨國公司研究的多層次性是公認的，卻沒有研究採取這多層次性的觀點。在這項研究中，我結合組織控制學和跨國公司的多層次性，並提出一個多層次跨國公司管理模型。這個項目有潛力提供新的見解去理解跨國公司組織管理對利益相關者的影響。

643610.label: Realisation of objectives
643610.value: In terms of the two objectives noted previously, I have satisfied both objectives by examining and demonstrating impacts of different control mechanisms used by the MNC and its agents, expatriate managers, on HCN managers’ attitudes, namely overall job satisfaction. In this study, we developed hypotheses relating two control mechanisms used by the expatriate managers and two controls used by the MNC headquarters on expatriate managers through an integration of organizational control literature with a cross-level theoretical perspective. We found a significant positive relationship between input control mechanism (i.e., planning behavior), and capability-based process (i.e., consulting behavior) control mechanism of expatriate managers on HCN managers’ job satisfaction. The findings contribute to the control literature by showing that control does not necessary imply negative consequences (Cardinal, 2001); a broader conceptualization of appropriate control mechanisms can actually promote positive outcomes, such as employees’ satisfaction. We currently have a manuscript under review (Takeuchi, Li, & Shay) from this research effort. Takeuchi, R., Li, J. T., & Shay, J. P. 643610.label: Major findings and research outcome
643610.value: By integrating organizational control literature with leadership theories, we advance a cross-level theorizing on the expatriate managerial control behaviors. We first examined the impact of two (input and process/behavioral) types of controls utilized by the expatriate managers on HCN managers’ overall job satisfaction. We also investigated the moderating effects of decision latitude and parent company commitment (two types of control used by MNCs on expatriate managers) on the aforementioned relationships, using survey data collected from expatriate general managers and HCNs. We found a significant positive relationship between input control mechanism (i.e., planning behavior), and process (i.e., consulting behavior) control mechanism of expatriate managers on HCN managers’ job satisfaction. The findings contribute to the control literature by showing that control does not necessary imply negative consequences; a broader conceptualization of appropriate control mechanisms can actually promote positive outcomes, such as employees’ satisfaction. This is perhaps one of the first studies to conceptualize expatriate managers’ behaviors from a control theory perspective, and to illustrate the influence of different types of control mechanisms on HCNs’ attitudes. Given that one of the major purposes of sending expatriates to foreign subsidiaries is to control the attitudes and behavior of host country nationals, this study contributes to the MNC literature by illustrating the mechanisms through which expatriate managers’ use of different control mechanisms would affect HCNs’ attitudes. Although the relationships between expatriate managers’ use of control mechanisms and HCNs’ attitudes are implied in much of MNC control literature, this study is the first to explicitly conceptualize and test these relationships. In addition, this study also contributes to expatriate literature by showing the impact of expatriate managers on HCNs. I am working on getting a manuscript published from this research project entitled "Configurational perspective on foreign subsidiary structures and its impact on expatriate general managers"(Takeuchi, R., Li, J. T., & Shay, J. P.), currently under 1st round review at Organization Science.

643610.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
643610.value: This study points out the importance of balance between formal and informal control in the organization. It is very important to keep a balance between the use of formal and informal control. Our findings illustrate the need for additional research that elucidates the complicated means through which different types of control mechanisms affect expatriate managers and HCNs. We believe that this study is the first step toward such understanding. Future research should extend this line of work and examine the impact of different types of controls MNC use on expatriate managers’ attitudes and behaviors, as well as how these controls may indirectly shape the attitudes and behaviors of HNCs. Another future research direction is to examine the differential impact of control mechanisms depending on the evolutionary stages of foreign subsidiaries. In other words, it may be the case that different control mechanisms are more effective at different stages of foreign subsidiary development.

643810.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
643810.value: This project examines the roles of information and financial constraints in creating barriers to agricultural sales. Small farmers in remote areas are often information-constrained: they lack the connections to larger wholesale markets that might inform them of arbitrage opportunities. They also tend to be credit-constrained: they lack collateral for formal loans, and so they rely on high-cost lending from local moneylenders. This also leaves them vulnerable to price fluctuations. Together, these constraints can force them to sell their produce early in the season, and to miss out on later, possibly higher prices. Further, many of the credit contracts tend to be interlinked; the moneylender is also a trader, and the production loan is repaid by selling the crop to him at a price lower than the market rate. This same trader-cum-moneylender is often also the farmer's chief source of market information, and thus the information and credit constraints work together to depress the farmer's revenues. We will conduct a randomized field experiment in a sample of villages in West Bengal, India. In randomly selected villages, we will publicly disseminate daily potato price information from local markets. In addition, we will provide subsidized credit to randomly selected farmers. A 2 x 2 cross-design of these two interventions will allow us to examine their independent as well as interactive effects on farmer sales and cropping behavior. Our insights will inform policy discussions in many parts of the developing world, including China, where the government has invested in cellular technology to help the development of agricultural markets. Even if information interventions are relatively cost effective, their effectiveness may well be enhanced by supplementing them with financial interventions. This can expand the menu of choices for policymakers: instead of two polar kinds of policies in isolation, they can consider combinations of them. 本項目研究信息和財務約束在妨礙農產品銷售中所起的作用。 在偏遠地區的小農戶往往受信息所限：他們難以接觸到更大的批發市場，從而錯過可能的套利機會。他們同時往往被信貸所約束：他們缺乏正規貸款所需之抵押品，所以只能依賴於當地的地下錢莊提供的高成本貸款。這也使他們更容易受到價格波動的影響。總之，這些因素迫使他們往往提前出售其農產品，從而錯過了以後可能更高的價格。此外，眾多的信貸合同往往是相互關聯的，債主同時也是一名商人，生產貸款的償還是通過以低於市場價向他出售作物而達成。同樣是這位商人兼債主，往往也充當了農民的市場信息的主要來源，這種信息和信貸約束的共同影響造成了農民收入的進一步緊縮。 我們將在印度的西孟加拉邦的村莊進行隨機抽樣試驗。在隨機選擇的村莊中，我們將公開發布每日當地市場的馬鈴薯價格信息。此外，我們將為隨機選擇的農民提供信貸補助。這兩項措施的 2 × 2交叉設計將使我們重新審視它們對農民銷售和種植行為的獨立以及交互影響。 我們的見解將在許多發展中國家及地區引起廣泛的政策討論，包括中國，該國政府已在手機技術方面做了投入以幫助發展農業市場。即使信息政策的相對成本較低，補助的財務干預可能會更好地增強其效果。這可以為決策者提供多樣化的選擇：他們可以考慮這些政策的組合，而不是分別來考慮它們。

643810.label: Realisation of objectives
643810.value: We have successfully conducted the proposed field experiment, which started in Fall 2010 and is still on-going with the help of some additional funding. We have created a two-year long household-level panel data set, and data collection is also still on-going. We have divided the project's research question into two broad sub-questions: (a) analysing the financial sustainability of the credit intervention from the lender's perspective, and (b) analysing the economic impact of the two interventions on the borrowers. We have made considerable progress on part (a). In particular, we have developed a theoretical model based on adverse selection, in the presence of a segmented informal credit market, that explains what type of borrowers are selected into our credit scheme. The predictions of this model in terms of the risk level of the borrowers and their repayment rates, have been successfully tested in the data, and implications for the financial sustainability of the scheme have been drawn out. With regard to (b) we have analysed the data on the effects on farmer sales, harvest, cropping decisions, revenues and incomes. These data will continue to be analysed further as more data come in. We also have developed some preliminary policy implications for how our credit scheme could boost agricultural incomes.

643810.label: Major findings and research outcome
643810.value: Our major findings are as follows: 1) A version of the alternative microcredit delivery mechanism that we designed, has proved to be successful in our field experiment. Our data show that the agent-intermediated lending approach, when implemented through traders (we call this TRAIL) has high take-up rates, and generates high repayment rates. 2) We have developed a theoretical model of adverse selection in the presence of a segmented informal credit market and used it to generate empirical predictions for the mechanism by which these high repayment rates came about. We show that the agents in the AIL scheme selected safe borrowers from within their own segment. We find no evidence of collusion between the agent and the borrowers. In contrast in the control group-based lending (GBL) scheme, borrowers were on average riskier. (This partially satisfies Objective 3.) 3) The TRAIL scheme is also relatively cost-effective: the MFI incurs substantially lower costs in administering it than in GBL. 4) TRAIL borrowers were on average wealthier than GBL borrowers. Thus the GBL scheme appears to be more pro-poor. 5) The TRAIL scheme generated large positive impacts on farmers' harvests, revenues and value-added. In contrast the GBL scheme did not generate significant impacts. Further theorising is needed to understand these differential impacts, to satisfy Objective 3 completely. 6) The average effects in 5) mask heterogeneity by landholding: farmers in the 0.5-1 acre land category have similar impacts under both the TRAIL and the GBL schemes. This is suggestive evidence that the TRAIL scheme outperforms GBL through successfully targeting the borrowers who are likely to have high returns to capital. 7) We are in the process of developing policy implications based on our research (in keeping with Objective 6). MFIs could use different credit delivery approaches to target different borrowers. The traditional group-based lending (GBL) approach attracts poor borrowers, and even they generate reasonably high repayment rates, although we do not find significant positive impacts on their cropping decisions, harvests or incomes. Still, it is possible that these loans help them to smooth consumption, and therefore are welfare-improving. On the other hand, the agent-based lending (AIL) approach targets borrowers with intermediate landholding, who expand their cultivation and harvests, and can earn high returns on the loans, which in turn should increase their incomes and alleviate their poverty. 8) Objective 5 has not been addressed yet. 9) A first working paper that has emerged from this project is available here: http://www.bm.ust.hk/econ/staff/AILPaper10March2013.pdf

643810.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
643810.value: Certain new questions arise as a result of our research. In particular -- a) What is the underlying reason why both GBL and TRAIL borrowers of similar land-size generate similar positive impacts of the microcredit schemes? One possibility is that landsize is positively correlated with unobserved ability, and AIL agents have this information and therefore select those borrowers into the scheme. Alternatively, the agricultural production function is S-shaped in land size, and the loan size in our scheme was much too small for the poorer borrowers to increase land size enough to overcome the poverty trap. We hope to extend our analysis to answer this question. b) How can the AIL scheme be made financially sustainable for the lender? How can we trade-off the incentive offered to agents for selecting good borrowers, with its costs to the lender, to arrive at a scheme that allows the lender to break even while continuing to generate positive outcomes? We are exploring the possibility of collaborating with a new larger microfinance institution to run a new experiment that will examine this question.

643810.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
643810.value: "Traditional" group-based (micro-)lending (GBL) schemes have recently come under criticism: they do not encourage risk-taking, there are contagious defaults, and high non-monetary costs for borrowers, and most importantly, no evidence that they alleviate poverty. We modify the scheme to employ "agents": local intermediaries who recommend borrowers to the lender, for individual liability loans. In this agent-intermediaed lending (AIL) scheme, loan durations are also extended to match the agricultural cycle. We find high take-up rates, continuation rates and repayment rates. Our analysis shows that agent select safe borrowers for the scheme, and do not collude with them. We also find significant positive impacts on borrowers' cultivation, harvests, revenues and value-added. However, the scheme targets borrowers of intermediate wealth, whereas the traditional scheme targets poorer households. This suggests that the AIL and GBL schemes could be used as complements to each other, each to target a different set of borrowers and deliver different outcomes: AIL schemes may help to raise incomes, whereas GBL schemes may help to smooth consumption.
